It was a great week for the Brewers. They won their fourth straight NL Central title and sixth in the last nine years, and also set another franchise record for wins in a single season, one year after setting the previous record. They now have a chance to win 100 games for the first time in club history this week and still have the top seed in the NL to play for.
The Rays swept the Athletics and won their series against the Red Sox last week to put some distance between themselves and the Yankees in the AL East race. The gap in the division is now six games, and even though the two rivals play each other four times during the final week of the season, it would take a massive collapse from Tampa Bay to upset the current standings. Because the Rays also currently lead the season series with the Yankees, 6-3, all they need is to win one of the four games in New York to take the division title. With Shane McClanahan still recovering from his forearm injury — his availability for the playoffs is up in the air — Freddy Peralta has stepped up to lead the pitching staff over the last few weeks. Across his last five starts, he’s allowed just three runs in 28 2/3 innings. That’s the kind of production the Rays were hoping to get when they acquired him at the trade deadline.

The Dodgers are getting all their pieces in place for the postseason. Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki will be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and Shohei Ohtani should follow on Wednesday. There’s a lingering question about Blake Snell’s status after he injured his groin last week, but it sounds like he’ll be able to make a start during the final weekend of the season. And even though the majority of the year has been a slog for Kyle Tucker, his bat seems to have finally woken up at the right time; he collected nine hits and three home runs last week.
Having won 13 of their last 14 games, the Padres are peaking at exactly the right moment. They’ve surged five games ahead of the Diamondbacks and one ahead of the Phillies in the NL Wild Card standings, and are now tied with the Cubs for the top spot. San Diego’s final series of the season against Arizona still looms large, especially if the Friars stumble against the Dodgers in the series beforehand. You’re probably familiar with Fernando Tatis Jr.’s hot streak — he blasted four home runs last week to bring his total in September up to eight — but the biggest contributor to the Padres’ success recently has been Ty France. He had 12 hits and a home run last week and has posted a fantastic 168 wRC+ during the second half of the season.
After a couple of years away from the top, the Braves are NL East champions again — it’s their seventh division title in the last nine years. Atlanta’s dominance this year has been a welcome return to form. Even though his season has been a bit up and down, Ronald Acuña Jr. is looking like the superstar that won the MVP back in 2023 again. Last week, he smacked three home runs, including a go-ahead grand slam on Saturday, and is running a 191 wRC+ in September.
A little more than a week after being activated off the IL, Aaron Judge is back on the shelf, this time with a calf injury sustained on Wednesday. His availability for the playoffs is still up in the air, though he’s confident that he’ll be able to return sooner rather than later. Thankfully, Jazz Chisholm Jr. should be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and there’s some confidence that Trent Grisham will also be ready to return for the postseason. It helps that Ben Rice has bounced back from a rough August to post a 192 wRC+ in September. Still, Judge’s injury is a major blow to the Yankees’ hopes for a deep October run.

Even though the Red Sox lost both of their series last week, they managed to clinch a postseason berth on Sunday. It’s the cap to a remarkable turnaround after the team looked completely lost in mid-June. Boston can officially secure the second Wild Card spot with a couple of wins against the Guardians this week. Then the team can turn its attention to the Yankees and the rematch of last year’s Wild Card matchup between these two historic rivals.
Nothing is going to come easy for the Phillies over the next few weeks. The team placed Jesús Luzardo on the IL last week with a shoulder injury, but thankfully, it sounds like he’ll be ready to pitch in the playoffs. But before they count their chickens, they need to actually clinch a playoff spot. Philadelphia is four games up on the Diamondbacks in the NL Wild Card race, but its upcoming opponents are no cake walk; the Phillies have the Brewers and Rays on the schedule to finish off the regular season. Facing two of the best teams in baseball is quite a test ahead of the postseason, and the Phillies haven’t exactly been playing well lately.
The biggest concern for the Cubs right now is the status of Alex Bregman. It would be a huge blow if the third baseman had to miss any significant amount of time at this point in the season. As for Crow-Armstrong, he’s two stolen bases away from joining the 40/40 club. item.content:encoded:
A scary scene took place on Sunday when Chicago Cubs star Alex Bregman was hit in the face by a foul ball and force to exit the game against the Cincinnati Reds. After the game, Bregman posted a photo on his Instagram, telling fans that he will be fine, but also showing the damage the foul ball did.
Bregman may ultimately end up being just fine in the next week, but there is at least a chance he could land on the injured list and miss the rest of the regular season while the Cubs try to zero in on clinching a playoff spot.
How Bregman's injury impacts Cubs, playoff race
The Cubs would have the top wild card spot if the regular season ended today. They begin a three-game series on Tuesday night against the Miami Marlins, while the San Diego Padres face the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Philadelphia Phillies face the Milwaukee Brewers.
By strength of schedule, the Cubs have the easiest week of the three teams in wild card spots. But without Bregman, things could get a little bit more difficult. They'll face Bregman's former team, the Boston Red Sox over the weekend.
This could potentially hurt their chances of securing the top wild card spot and knock them down a bit in the standings, creating room for Philadelphia and San Diego to climb to the top. And if the Cubs are without Bregman at all in the postseason, then they will have tougher time getting out of the wild card round, as they could find themselves playing one of the other two wild card teams, or possibly even the Atlanta Braves.
The Cubs lost the NLDS last year to the Milwaukee Brewers, and they'll hope to make a deeper run this October, but any time without Bregman will make that task all the more difficult.
Bregman could be back in time for the postseason, so that could give the Cubs a better chance, but the timing of the injury certainly isn't good, especially with Chicago still trying to secure their wild card berth now that Milwaukee has already won the National League Central. It's going to be difficult to stay hot if he ends up landing on the injured list.
It will be interesting to see how he recovers and if he will be able to recover in time to help the Cubs in the playoffs.

The Chicago Cubs may have dominated the afternoon on Sunday against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ballpark, but the victory quickly became secondary after Alex Bregman took a foul ball to the face that caused him to leave the game. He's since given update that he's okay, and that he's on track to make a full recovery. But there's one heck of a shiner on his face.
It was a dismal scene, considering that Bregman wasn't even involved in the play at the time. He was simply an on-deck batter waiting to come up to bat. A slight bump off of the bat of Nico Hoerner, and suddenly a four seam fastball that didn't mean anything suddenly meant a great deal to a lot of people.
Bregman is almost surely going to miss time due to this if the photos he posted are anything to go off of. Bregman himself seems to be in good spirits, but there's no way he can play with his eye swollen shut.
The Cubs are currently 87-69, and tightly locked in the Wild Card race with the San Diego Padres and the Philadelphia Phillies. Over the last few days, little has changed between the three, with the Cubs remaining constantly tied for the top spot. With the Cubs unable to break away and hold the lead down, the end of the season is going to be a barn-burner for who stands when the dust settles.
Bregman is batting .262 right now with 26 home runs and 89 RBIs through 153 games. Beyond that production, he's one of the premier corner infielders in the game, meaning his glove on the field will be missed. The Cubs are lucky enough to have Pedro Ramirez and Matt Shaw waiting in the wings, but they'll certainly want to have their starting third baseman back.
The Cubs have yet to release a timeline, but seeing as it's not even been 24 hours since the injury took place, that's not particularly surprising. The team will undoubtedly wish to get Bregman back on the field when he's ready to play, but at this late stage int he season, time is of the essence.
Hopefully Bregman can make a full recovery and be ready to go for the first tastes of October baseball. But for now, the Cubs need to focus on maintaining that top Wild Card spot, because it could hold significant home-field advantage when it really matters.

item.content:encoded:
It’s time for both sides of this great baseball town to come together.
No, not the fans. We know better than to ask for that.
Rather, we mean the Cubs and White Sox themselves, for — a doff of the cap and a drumroll, please — the Sun-Times’ 2026 All-City Team is here.
Beat writers Vinnie Duber (Cubs) and James Fegan (Sox) joined frequent baseball scribe Jeff Agrest and yours truly in selecting a 17-man team: one player at each position in the field, a designated hitter, four starting pitchers, three relievers — one of them designated as closer — and a manager.
Four ironclad rules guided our process:
1. This is a 2026 honor. Reputation doesn’t matter.
2. If it’s too close to call at certain positions, lean into which players we’d rather write into a playoff lineup.
3. All players must appear at their primary positions. No exceptions!
4. OK, fine, Alex Bregman and Miguel Vargas both need to be in there somehow. Besides, if we journalists followed the rules, how would everybody know to hate us?
Our team:
SP1: Sean Burke, Sox
Leads Chicago starters in ERA, strikeouts, opponent batting average — closest we’ve got to an ace.
SP2: Shota Imanaga, Cubs
Other than the gopher balls — so many gopher balls — lefty has been effective.
SP3: Davis Martin, Sox
Sox were 10-1 over his first 11 starts. Finishing kick has been strong, too. (As for in between, don’t ask.)
SP4: Matthew Boyd, Cubs
Still one guy who — if locked in — can get you to the seventh inning of a playoff game.
C: Carson Kelly, Cubs
Good hitter, even better with men in scoring position. Not an All-Star, but we’ll take him.
1B: Munetaka Murakami, Sox
Hamstring injury derailed spectacular start. Still, top 10 in AL in homers, walks is big-time.
2B: Chase Meidroth, Sox
Sorry, Nico Hoerner, but this was an easy call. Meidroth has simply been the better batsman.
3B: Alex Bregman, Cubs
One of the best second halves in baseball, combined with stellar glove work. Tough call, though.
SS: Dansby Swanson, Cubs
Just too great on “D” — and Colson Montgomery didn’t get on base enough to unseat him.
LF: Tristan Peters, Sox
South Side’s best outfielder — an All-Star, don’t forget — gets bumped over by you-know-who.
CF: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
But you knew this already. Not bad, Mr. MVP.
RF: Seiya Suzuki, Cubs
His RISP work wasn’t the best, but you take the offensive totals every time.
DH: Miguel Vargas, Sox
Sox’ MVP — there’s no debate about that — simply has to be in our lineup.
RP: Bryan Hudson, Sox
Quality lefty with multiple impressive scoreless streaks and pinpoint control all second half.
RP: Sean Newcomb, Sox
Lefty hangs on to a spot despite a rough September.
Closer: Grant Taylor, Sox
The best reliever in town and the only sane choice for this role.
Manager: Craig Counsell, Cubs
Potentially winning 90 despite one pitching problem after another is nothing to sneeze at.
DISSENSIONS IN THE RANKS
In the end, we were in unison on all but three positions. Fegan backed Vargas at third base and Will Venable at manager, and I wanted Sam Antonacci in left.
Fegan on Vargas: Bregman and Vargas are statistically even, so let’s get sentimental. Vargas has been the rock of a Sox offense otherwise defined by streaks. He’s the proof of concept of their newfound ability to improve hitters. A universally beloved bilingual glue guy in a loose clubhouse, Vargas is the team MVP who laughs hard and works harder. Without him, Sox leadership is talking “meaningful progress” rather than playoffs.
Greenberg on Antonacci: His defense is more mosh pit than ballet, but throw him off his spot because of it? Come on, man. He’s always on base, hits in the clutch and plays with his rear end on fire. How do you not love a young cat with a perverse desire to stand in front of 96 mph and get drilled by it? These Sox aren’t these Sox without his signature brand of — how to put it? — Antonacciness.
Fegan on Venable: His in-game moves miss the mark at times; inarguable since he readily fesses up without prompting. But with how naturally fans and commentators have shifted to second-guessing every crucial move in a division chase, it might surprise locally how well Venable does in AL manager of the year voting, or how the baseball world still views his team cracking the playoffs as coaching alchemy, or how much his constant tinkering is not unique but actually–gasp!–the Sox adhering to modern trends.
Contributing: James Fegan, Vinnie Duber, Jeff Agrest

Alex Bregman vivió un momento de preocupación durante la victoria de los Chicago Cubs por 9-1 sobre los Cincinnati Reds, luego de recibir un pelotazo en el rostro mientras se encontraba en el círculo de espera del Great American Ball Park.
El incidente ocurrió en la parte alta de la cuarta entrada, con dos outs. Michael Busch, compañero de Bregman, conectó una pelota de foul que terminó golpeando al tercera base en el pómulo izquierdo, debajo del ojo.
Bregman se dirigió inmediatamente al dugout y ya no regresó al encuentro. Matt Shaw entró en su lugar, mientras el cuerpo médico de los Cubs atendía al jugador.
La escena generó preocupación entre sus compañeros debido a que el pelotazo impactó directamente en el rostro.

El jugador fue trasladado a un hospital
Después de abandonar el terreno de juego, Bregman fue llevado a un hospital local para someterse a radiografías y una tomografía computarizada, con el objetivo de conocer el alcance de la lesión.
El manager de los Cubs, Craig Counsell, explicó que el pelotero tenía una cortada debajo del ojo, sangrado nasal y una inflamación considerable en la zona donde recibió el impacto.
“Tenía una cortada debajo del ojo. Le sangraba un poco la nariz. Está bastante hinchado”, explicó Counsell tras el encuentro. El manager también señaló que inicialmente pensó que el pelotero podía haberse fracturado la nariz, aunque todavía esperaban los resultados de los estudios médicos.

Bregman muestra su rostro y manda mensaje a los aficionados
Horas después del incidente, Bregman utilizó sus redes sociales para compartir una fotografía en la que mostró la inflamación y el golpe que sufrió en el lado izquierdo del rostro.

“Gracias por todos sus mensajes. Estaré de regreso”, escribió Bregman en Instagram.

Por ahora, los Cubs deberán esperar la evaluación médica para determinar el alcance de la lesión y cuándo podrá volver a jugar. El equipo se encuentra en plena lucha por un lugar en la postemporada, por lo que la disponibilidad de Bregman será un tema a seguir en los próximos días.

The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

CINCINNATI -- The Chicago Cubs were somber after they defeated the Cincinnati Reds, 9-1, at Great American Ball Park on Sunday because Chicago was thinking about third baseman Alex Bregman, who was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of teammate Michael Busch.
Bregman was injured in the fourth inning with two outs. With the count, 1-2, Busch checked his swing at a pitch thrown by Reds right-hander Luis Mey. The ball made contact with Busch's bat, however, and then hit Bregman while he was in the on-deck circle. Bregman then ran towards the end of the Cubs' dugout before finally going into the clubhouse to get looked at by the team’s trainer.
Bregman was taken to a nearby hospital for X-rays and a CT scan, but the Cubs have yet to announce the seriousness of Bregman’s injury.
“I don’t know anything more than that,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell told reporters. “He had a cut under his eye. He was bleeding from his nose a little bit. It’s pretty swollen. It was below the eye. I honestly thought it hit him in the nose. I thought he had a broken nose, but I knew it hit him somewhere in the face. It’s just an unfortunate accident. I’m hoping and praying he is all right.
“We have to get good results from the hospital first. [Bregman] got hit in the face, so you are worried about his general well-being first. If we get a good report, we’ll move to the next step. I want to get a good report.”
Bregman is in his first season with the Cubs after signing a five-year, $175 million contract last January. He is having a productive season with the Cubbies, slashing .262/.352/.452 with 26 home runs and 89 RBI.
Before Sunday’s game, Bregman spoke to Yardbarker about his first season with the Cubs.
"The first half didn’t start out how I wanted it. (I) kept fighting. (I) trusted the process,” Bregman said. “I felt like myself over the last two months. That’s what I expect from myself. I’ve also been super thrilled to be in a position to continue to play postseason baseball, play meaningful games in October. I’ve been fortunate to do that every year of my career, which I don’t take lightly. I’m happy that we put ourselves in the position, so far, to be in.”
Bregman even had a word to say about teammate Pete Crow-Armstrong. To Bregman, PCA is the National League Most Valuable Player, and he has the stats to back it up.
Entering Tuesday’s action against the Marlins, Crow-Armstrong is leading the Majors with 10.5 wins above replacement (per FanGraphs) and 118 runs scored. He could also become the seventh player in MLB history to reach the 40-40 plateau.
“He has been the best player in the sport. It’s not even close,” Bregman said about PCA.

item.content:encoded:
Un momento completamente accidental encendió las alarmas en las Grandes Ligas. Alex Bregman, tercera base de los Chicago Cubs, terminó en el hospital después de recibir un fuerte pelotazo en el rostro durante el juego contra los Cincinnati Reds, pese a que ni siquiera se encontraba bateando cuando ocurrió el impacto.
¿Cómo ocurrió el accidente de Alex Bregman?
El incidente se produjo este domingo 20 de septiembre en el Great American Ball Park, cuando Michael Busch estaba en la caja ante los lanzamientos del dominicano Luis Mey. El pelotero de Chicago realizó un swing contenido y alcanzó a desviar la bola de foul, que tomó una trayectoria inesperada hacia donde Bregman esperaba su turno.
Con dos outs en la cuarta entrada, la pelota golpeó directamente a Bregman en el pómulo izquierdo, debajo del ojo. El antesalista reaccionó inmediatamente, soltó su bat y caminó hacia el dugout mientras se cubría la zona afectada con una mano.
La escena generó preocupación entre sus compañeros debido a la fuerza y ubicación del impacto. El manager de los Cubs, Craig Counsell, reveló posteriormente que el jugador presentaba una cortada debajo del ojo, inflamación y también sangrado por la nariz.
“Es un accidente terrible. Esperamos que esté bien”, señaló el estratega, quien admitió que inicialmente creyó que su pelotero podía tener la nariz fracturada debido a la violencia del golpe.
Chicago decidió retirarlo inmediatamente del encuentro. Matt Shaw entró como bateador emergente, mientras Pedro Ramírez posteriormente pasó a cubrir la tercera base. Los Cubs terminaron imponiéndose 9-1 sobre Cincinnati.
Alex Bregman fue trasladado al hospital
Debido a que la bola alcanzó una zona particularmente delicada, Bregman fue enviado a un hospital para someterse a radiografías y una tomografía computarizada (CT) con el objetivo de conocer la gravedad de la lesión y descartar daños mayores.
Michael Busch reconoció que continuar jugando después del episodio resultó complicado. El beisbolista explicó que todo sucedió en cuestión de segundos y manifestó su preocupación debido a que cualquier golpe en la cabeza genera alarma dentro del diamante.
Horas después, el propio Bregman dio señales alentadoras mediante sus redes sociales. El estadounidense publicó una fotografía donde apareció con el ojo izquierdo completamente inflamado, moretones y restos de sangre alrededor del rostro, una imagen que evidenció la fuerza del impacto.
Pese a lo aparatoso de su aspecto, acompañó la publicación con un breve mensaje para tranquilizar a sus seguidores: “Gracias por todos los mensajes. Volveré”.
El accidente llegó además durante una campaña importante para Bregman con los Cubs. El tercera base registra promedio de .262, 26 cuadrangulares y 89 carreras impulsadas en la temporada 2026, por lo que su evolución médica será seguida de cerca por Chicago en la recta final de la campaña.

item.content:encoded:
The Cubs are as close to securing a trip back to the postseason as possible.
The North Siders need just a single win, or a single D-backs loss, over the regular season’s final week to clinch a spot in the NL Wild Card round.
Who will the Cubs play? And where will those games be played? Those questions won’t be answered until next weekend, most likely.
But with just six games remaining until playoff baseball, who will the Cubs need to step up in order to make a run at the World Series in a National League field filled with strong contenders such as the Brewers, Dodgers and Braves?
Here’s a look at who the Cubs need to do their part to get back to the Fall Classic for the first time since 2016:
Who will step up at the back end of the 'pen?
Who will close games? This is by far the Cubs’ biggest, and potentially most important, question that needs to be answered. Will it be Jacob Webb, who leads the team with nine saves, or will former closer Daniel Palencia, who just spun two scoreless innings in one of his most impressive outings of the year, be able to take that role? Manager Craig Counsell, who has used 14 pitchers to record saves this season, will be tasked with piecing together a bullpen that has limited experience in those situations.
The Cubs need Webb, who spun a scoreless outing in 24 straight appearances from June to August, to get back into form after allowing 11 runs over his past 7 2/3 innings (nine games). If Palencia, who has thrown 6 1/3 straight scoreless innings, can also replicate his success from 2025, it could be a major boost for a club that entered Cincinnati converting just four of its past 12 save opportunities.
Deadline acquisition Ryan Zeferjahn and lefty Ryan Rolison could also play a big factor late in games, but there’s also a secret weapon waiting out in the bullpen …
Can Cabrera be a reliable relief option?
That brings us to Edward Cabrera, who returned from a recurring blister injury on his pitching hand on Sept. 15 in a multi-inning relief role. That will be his job going forward as the Cubs hope shorter outings can not only keep him healthy, but potentially provide a small uptick in velocity. Cabrera’s first relief experience had mixed results (two runs in 2 1/3 IP), but he came out of the bullpen Sunday and tossed a scoreless inning on just nine pitches.
The best-case scenario of this temporary move to the bullpen? Cabrera turns into this year’s version of the Dodgers’ Roki Sasaki, which would immediately help stabilize the back end of the Cubs’ bullpen. Cabrera’s season hasn’t gone to plan, posting a 5.68 ERA in 15 starts between three stints on the injured list, but he still has a chance to make a significant impact when it matters most.
PCA still doing MVP things in October
Is it really fair to ask more of Pete Crow-Armstrong? After going yard again Sunday, the Cubs slugger is tied with Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber for the most home runs in the Major Leagues. He leads Chicago in batting average (.280), homers (45), RBIs (107), stolen bases (38), runs scored (118), on-base percentage (.371), hits (170), triple (eight) and games played (156). Got all that? Simply put, he’s put together one of the most impressive offensive seasons in Cubs history and he’s not done.
But he will need others to contribute in October. While run production starts with Crow-Armstrong, even if he performs to his NL MVP front-runner ability, he can’t do it all himself. The North Siders have to count on Seiya Suzuki, Dansby Swanson, Ian Happ, Alex Bregman and Michael Busch below him in the lineup to generate scoring chances.
Holmes stepping up as playoff ace
Clay Holmes and Matthew Boyd are the clear No. 1 and No. 2 options for the playoffs, but Counsell hasn’t yet revealed who will pitch in the all-important Game 1. Holmes had a strong August (1.55 ERA in five starts) in his return to the big leagues after missing nearly three months with a right fibula fracture, but he’s allowed 16 ER in just 15 1/3 IP across three starts in September (9.39 ERA).
That’s a worrying trend for a club with limited starting options in the postseason, but Shota Imanaga has stabilized recently after a down stretch in August, and veteran Kevin Gausman can provide multiple innings in whatever role the Cubs need during the postseason.

The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |

For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman shared a graphic selfie Sunday after suffering a frightening facial injury from a foul ball during an MLB game.
Bregman was struck during the fourth inning of Chicago's 9-1 win over the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park. Teammate Michael Busch fouled a pitch from Luis Mey, and the ball bounced into Bregman while he stood near the on-deck circle.
Bregman immediately left the game with blood visible on his face. He later underwent hospital testing after the ball struck him near his cheekbone.
The selfie, which he shared on his Instagram, showed significant swelling around Bregman's eye, along with facial cuts and a nosebleed. Especially the area below his eye had turned slightly black. He also included a message for supporters: "Thanks for all the messages, y'all. I'll be back 🙏."
Cubs manager Craig Counsell described the incident as a "terrible, terrible accident." He said the team's priority was getting positive medical results after Bregman was taken to the hospital.
The injury came during an important stretch for Chicago. The Cubs entered Sunday chasing a postseason berth and remained positioned for a National League wild-card spot.
Cubs must manage Alex Bregman's absence carefully
Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman (3) walks off the field after getting hit by a foul ball in the fourth inning in the game against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Bregman had already contributed during Sunday's game before leaving. He delivered an RBI single in the first inning, helping Chicago build an early lead.
After Bregman exited, Matt Shaw replaced him as a pinch-hitter. Pedro Ramirez shifted to third base while Shaw moved to second.
The Cubs continued producing offensively without their veteran third baseman. Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run, while Michael Conforto and Seiya Suzuki also homered.
Chicago now faces a balance between its postseason push and Bregman's recovery. His defensive stability and veteran experience remain valuable during the final week.
Counsell said Bregman's general well-being came before baseball considerations. "I want to get a good report first," the manager said.
Bregman's message offered some optimism, but his return timeline remains unclear. The Cubs will need to await further medical updates before determining his availability.

CINCINNATI -- Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman had to leave Sunday’s 9-1 victory against the Reds at Great American Ball Park after getting hit in the left cheek bone by a foul ball from teammate Michael Busch.
With two outs in the fourth inning, Busch was at the plate when he half-swung at a pitch thrown by Reds right-hander Luis Mey. Busch fouled off the pitch and the ball hit Bregman while he was in the on-deck circle. Bregman immediately went into the dugout, and he was replaced by pinch-hitter Matt Shaw.
Bregman was sent to the hospital for X-rays and a CT scan, but there wasn't any initial word after the game regarding what kind of damage was done.
“I don’t know anything more than that,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said. “He had a cut under his eye. He was bleeding from his nose a little bit. It’s pretty swollen. It was below the eye. I honestly thought it hit him in the nose. I thought he had a broken nose, but I knew it hit him somewhere in the face. It’s just an unfortunate accident. I’m hoping and praying he is all right.
“We have to get good results from the hospital first. [Bregman] got hit in the face, so you are worried about his general well-being first. If we get a good report, we’ll move to the next step. I want to get a good report.”
Shaw drew a walk, then remained in the game to play second base, with Pedro Ramírez shifting to third base.
The Cubs, who were winning 5-0 at the time of Bregman's exit, can clinch a postseason berth if the D-backs lose to the Yankees on Sunday afternoon.

NEW YORK (AP) — Cristopher Sánchez earned his major league-leading 18th win Sunday, leading the Philadelphia Phillies to a 7-2 victory over the New York Mets.
The Phillies (86-70), who salvaged a split of the four-game series, entered Sunday in the third National League wild-card spot, one game behind the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four games clear of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Sánchez surrendered six hits — including Bo Bichette’s sixth-inning homer — and struck out six over 6 1/3 innings as he snapped a tie with the Boston Red Sox’s Sonny Gray for the big league lead in wins.

The last Phillies pitcher to lead the majors in wins was Steve Carlton with 23 in 1982.
Justin Crawford had a three-run triple and Luis Arraez finished with two RBIs. Alec Bohm and Trea Turner each had run-scoring hits. Kyle Schwarber tied a career high with four walks.
Rookie Jonah Tong (2-2) gave up four runs and struck out five in 4 2/3 innings for the last-place Mets, who finished 36-45 at home — their worst record at Citi Field since the 2013 team went 33-48.
PIRATES 4, ROYALS 3
PITTSBURGH (AP) — Rafael Flores Jr. hit the go-ahead two-run home run in the eighth inning to help Pittsburgh to a win over Kansas City and complete a series sweep.
After Ryan O’Hearn led off with a single to center, Flores sent a slider from Nate Pearson (2-3) into the left-field bleachers for his 10th homer this season.
Pittsburgh rallied with a two-run homer in the eighth for a second straight day. Brandon Lowe had his 33rd of the season in a 6-5 win Saturday.
Carmen Mlodzinki (8-7) got the win. He allowed two runs and three hits in three innings. The reliever gave up a pinch-hit, two-run home run to Vinnie Pasquantino that gave Kansas City a 3-2 lead with two outs in the seventh.
Mason Montgomery earned his 16th save. He retired the first two batters in the ninth before Luke Maile hit a double and took third on a fielding error by Jake Mangum. Montgomery got Isaac Collins to fly out to right to strand Maile.
The Royals went ahead 1-0 in the first inning with three straight singles off Lake Bachar. Bobby Witt Jr. beat out a groundball to second baseman Lowe. He moved to third on a single to right from Jac Caglianone and scored when Perez shot one through the middle of the infield.
RAYS 5, RED SOX 1
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay crept closer to the AL East title with a victory over Boston.
The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees.
Boston would have clinched a playoff spot with a victory. The Red Sox, who were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East on June 24, have since gone 52-25. They could still wrap up a spot Sunday with a Houston loss.
Jax (8-10) allowed three singles and worked out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning by striking out Roman Anthony. Cole Sulser, Brody Hopkins and Steven Matz each pitched an inning of scoreless relief.
Boston’s Trevor Story spoiled the shutout in the ninth with a one-out home run off right-hander Ty Johnson.
The Rays scored four first-inning runs off left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-7). Jonny DeLuca smashed a two-run, bases-loaded double down the left-field line and Chandler Simpson followed with a two-run single. Sandoval began the inning by walking Yandy Diaz and Ryan Vilade, then surrendering a single to Junior Caminero.
CUBS 9, REDS 1
CINCINNATI (AP) — Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run as Chicago moved closer to clinching a postseason berth with a victory over Cincinnati.
Chicago (87-69) reduced its magic number to one and could wrap up a berth if the Diamondbacks lose to the Yankees later Sunday.
The Cubs began the day tied with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies for the top NL wild-card spot which would earn them home-field advantage in the wild-card round. The Cubs own the tiebreakers over the Diamondbacks, Padres, and Phillies.
Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman left Sunday’s game in the fourth inning after being struck in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch while standing near the on-deck circle.
Cubs left-hander David Peterson (9-8) allowed a run on three hits in seven innings with one walk and seven strikeouts.
The Cubs loaded the bases with one out in the third. Ian Happ singled in a run and Nico Hoerner walked to force in another to extend Chicago’s lead to 3-0. Pedro Ramirez’s two-run single made the score 5-0.
Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder (6-12) allowed five earned runs on six hits with three walks and three strikeouts.
CARDINALS 5, NATIONALS 3
ST. LOUIS (AP) — Iván Herrera hit a pair of home runs, and Leo Bernal also homered as St. Louis scored three runs in the eighth inning to come from behind and beat Washington.
Bernal hit his fifth homer of the season off Yovanny Cruz (0-2) after Erik Tolman walked Jordan Walker with two outs in the eighth inning.
Herrera hit his second homer of the game and 18th of the season to tie the game at 3-all after hitting a solo shot in the first inning.
It was Herrera’s third career multi-homer game and second this season after going deep twice on June 13 at Minnesota.
Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless eighth inning for St. Louis, and Riley O’Brien pitched a perfect ninth to earn his National League-leading 38th save.
Cardinals starter Quinn Mathews allowed three runs on seven hits and two walks in a career-high seven innings.
Jake Irvin allowed two runs on three hits and had eight strikeouts in 5 1/3 innings for the Nationals.

CINCINNATI – Al comenzar el domingo el último juego de la serie contra los Rojos, el jardinero central de los Cachorros, Pete Crow-Armstrong, venía de un fin de semana frustrante, al irse de 10-0 con cuatro ponches en los primeros dos encuentros de la serie. Pero dejó atrás esos días complicados al quedarse a un triple de completar el ciclo y ayudar a Chicago a aplastar 9-1 a los Rojos en el Great American Ball Park.
La victoria dejó a los Cachorros un poco más cerca de la postemporada, pero necesitan que los Yankees derroten a los D-backs más tarde la tarde del domingo para asegurar oficialmente su boleto a octubre. Chicago tiene a su favor el criterio de desempate por enfrentamientos directos ante los Padres (5-1) y los Filis (6-1), los dos equipos que están por debajo en la lucha por los Comodines de la Liga Nacional, lo que le da ventaja en la pelea por obtener la localía para la Serie del Comodín, que comienza el 29 de septiembre.
Crow-Armstrong se fue de 5-3 con un jonrón y dos carreras impulsadas. Todo comenzó en el primer inning ante el derecho de los Rojos, Rhett Lowder. Crow-Armstrong conectó un sencillo al jardín derecho y luego se robó la segunda base, quedando a dos estafadas de lograr la primera temporada 40-40 en la historia de los Cachorros. Finalmente anotó con un sencillo de Alex Bregman, quien salió del juego en el cuarto episodio tras recibir en la cabeza el impacto de una pelota de foul conectada por su compañero Michael Busch.
Chicago anotó cuatro carreras ante Lowder en el tercer episodio, con PCA como principal protagonista. Abrió el inning con un doble y anotó la segunda rayita del juego gracias a un sencillo de Ian Happ. Fue el 30mo doble de la temporada para PCA, convirtiéndose en el 10mo jugador en la historia de Grandes Ligas con al menos una campaña de 40 o más jonrones, 30 o más dobles y 30 o más bases robadas, uniéndose al venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr., Jeff Bagwell (dos veces), Ryan Braun, Ellis Burks, el cubano José Canseco, Shohei Ohtani, Alex Rodríguez, el dominicano Alfonso Soriano y Larry Walker.
Crow-Armstrong luego conectó un cuadrangular en el quinto capítulo, su 45to de la temporada, para igualar a Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de MLB.
La estrella de los Cachorros tuvo una última oportunidad de conseguir el triple que le faltaba para completar el ciclo en el octavo acto ante Carson Spiers, pero elevó al campocorto dominicano Elly De La Cruz para el primer out de la entrada.

item.content:encoded:
After going 0-for-10 with four strikeouts in the first two games of this series, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong had himself another big day in the third contest. PCA singled, doubled, homered and stole a base and helped lead the Cubs to a 9-1 blowout of the Reds, a victory tempered by a freak injury to Alex Bregman. More on the latter anon, first let’s wrap this win.
The Cubs got on the board in the first inning. PCA led off the game with a single and stole second, his 38th [VIDEO].
The Cubs extended their lead in the third. PCA led off with a double. A note on that double from BCB’s JohnW53:
With his third-inning double, Pete Crow-Armstrong has at least 30 homers, doubles and steals.
Only one Cub had done that before: PCA, last year.
Forty players on other teams have done it, 12 of them also multiple times. PCA is among 10 with two. Alfonso Soriano did it four times; Barry Bonds and Jose Ramirez, three.
It was noted on the Marquee broadcast that PCA’s 40-HR, 30-double, 30-steal year is the first ever by a MLB center fielder — nope, not Willie Mays, not Ken Griffey Jr., no one, until now. I’ve said it before, but don’t ever forget what you are seeing from Pete this year — it is truly historic.
Anyway, PCA then went to third on a ground out by Seiya Suzuki. The Cubs then loaded the bases on walks drawn by Michael Busch and Bregman.
Per the Marquee broadcast, that’s 22 bases-loaded walks for the Cubs this year, the most in MLB.
With the bases still loaded, Michael Conforto struck out, but Pedro Ramirez followed with a two-run single to make it 5-0 [VIDEO].
Now to the Bregman incident in the fourth inning. With two out, Busch hit a foul ball that struck Bregman, who was in the on-deck circle, in the face. Bregman immediately left the game and was replaced by Matt Shaw. Here’s what that looked like [VIDEO].
Per Craig Counsell’s postgame remarks, the ball hit Bregman in the cheekbone, which is swollen. There was also a facial cut, but we don’t know anything beyond that. Hopefully it’s not too serious and Bregman doesn’t have a concussion.
While all this was going on, David Peterson was sailing along, striking out seven over the first four innings. The Reds made it 5-1 on a solo homer by JJ Bleday in the fourth.
The Cubs got that run right back in the fifth on a solo homer by Michael Conforto, his 15th [VIDEO].
If you’re keeping track:
Kyle Tucker, 16 HR, 515 AB
Michael Conforto, 15 HR, 294 AB
That blast tied PCA with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead. The Cubs also lead MLB in home runs with 217; as noted on the Marquee broadcast, the last time the Cubs led all of baseball in home runs was 1958, led by Ernie Banks with 47 in his first MVP season.
Peterson completed six innings, allowing three hits and just the one run on Bleday’s homer. Here are his seven strikeouts [VIDEO].
More on Peterson’s afternoon from BCB’s JohnW53:
David Peterson’s quality start was his fifth as a Cub, fourth most on the team. Shota Imanaga has 14, as many as the next two combined: Matthew Boyd, eight, and Colin Rea, six. Edward Cabrera and Jameson Taillon both have four. Five others have one to three.
Peterson could be a valuable weapon in the postseason, either as a starter or out of the bullpen.
The Cubs weren’t done homering, either. After Caleb Thielbar threw a scoreless seventh, Suzuki lofted his 25th into the batter’s eye to make it 9-1 [VIDEO].
More on recent Cubs home runs from John:
With their three home runs, the Cubs have hit nine in their last four games (three, one, two, three). They had hit 12 in their previous 14 games, since smacking a team-record nine at home vs. the Brewers on Aug. 31.
Edward Cabrera was given the eighth inning, a good low-leverage situation. He allowed a leadoff single and after retiring the next hitter, another Reds batter reached on an error by Ramirez. But Cabrera got Elly De La Cruz to hit into an inning-ending double play.
Colin Rea finished up with a 1-2-3 ninth, his first game action in 11 days, on just eight pitches. Here’s the final out [VIDEO].
The Cubs will clinch a postseason berth if the Yankees defeat the Diamondbacks Sunday, a game that’s just begun at the time of this recap. The Padres, tied with the Cubs for the top wild card spot with the Cubs holding the tiebreaker, are playing the Marlins in a contest in San Diego that’s also just underway. The Phillies defeated the Mets Sunday, so the Cubs still lead Philadelphia by a game. Thanks to the Mets for taking two of the four games from the Phillies over the weekend.
The Cubs have Monday off, then open the final regular season home series Tuesday evening against the Marlins at Wrigley Field. Kevin Gausman will start for the Cubs and Janson Junk will go for Miami. Game time Tuesday is 6:40 p.m. CT and TV coverage will be via Marquee Sports Network.

CINCINNATI – Entering Sunday’s finale against the Reds, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong had a frustrating weekend, going 0-for-10 with four strikeouts over the first two games of the series. But he made up for those difficult days by coming a triple shy of the cycle and helping Chicago pound the Reds, 9-1, at Great American Ball Park.
The victory helped bring the Cubs an inch closer to the postseason, but they need the Yankees to beat the D-backs later Sunday afternoon to officially clinch October baseball. Chicago owns the head-to-head tiebreaker over the Padres (5-1) and the Phillies (6-1), the two teams below them in the NL Wild Card race, giving them the upper hand to earn home-field advantage for the Wild Card Series starting Sept. 29.
Crow-Armstrong went 3-for-5 with a homer and two RBIs. It all started in the first inning against Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder. Crow-Armstrong singled to right field and then stole second base, putting him two steals shy of the first 40-40 season in Cubs franchise history. He eventually scored on a single by Alex Bregman, who left the game in the fourth after getting hit in the head by a foul ball from teammate Michael Busch.
Chicago scored four runs off Lowder in the third frame, and it was PCA who led the charge. He led off with a double and scored the second run of the game on a single by Ian Happ. It was PCA’s 30th double of the season, making him the 10th player in Major League Baseball history to notch 40-plus homers, 30-plus doubles and 30-plus stolen bases in a season at least once, joining Ronald Acuña Jr., Jeff Bagwell (twice), Ryan Braun, Ellis Burks, Jose Canseco, Shohei Ohtani, Alex Rodriguez, Alfonso Soriano and Larry Walker.
Crow-Armstrong later homered in the fifth for his 45th blast of the season, tying him with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead.
The Cubs star got one last chance to tally the triple that would complete his cycle in the eighth against Carson Spiers, but he popped up to shortstop Elly De La Cruz for the first out of the inning.

item.content:encoded:
One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run.
While many key contributors struggled in the first half of 2026, several have picked it up big time since the All-Star break, lifting their clubs to late-season success.
Here are 10 players -- five hitters and five pitchers -- who have turned things around in the second half.
All stats are through Saturday's games unless otherwise specified.
Hitters
Alex Bregman, Cubs
For as good as National League MVP Award favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong has been lately, it’s actually Bregman who entered Saturday leading all qualifying hitters with a 168 wRC+ in the second half. The third baseman has a .298/.376/.609 slash line since the All-Star break, with his 17 second-half homers tied for fourth most in MLB.
Batting just .241 with nine home runs and a .695 OPS prior to the break, Bregman hadn’t exactly been meeting expectations after signing a five-year, $175 million deal with the Cubs. Now, though, he is up to 5.1 FanGraphs WAR, his highest total since 2022 (5.4). He’s been a big reason the Cubs are currently on track to host an NL Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field, and he will be a key bat in the middle of Chicago’s lineup in the postseason.
Steven Kwan, Guardians
With this week’s series win over the White Sox, the Guardians have surged into first place in the AL Central, in large part thanks to their leadoff hitter’s resurgence. In addition to his strong defense in left field -- Kwan has won four straight AL Gold Gloves in left to begin his career -- Kwan has been on fire at the plate.
After a disappointing first-half slash line of .225/.332/.282, including a .188 batting average in May, Kwan ranks second among qualifiers with a .347 average and is tied with Yordan Alvarez for first with a .435 on-base percentage in the second half. He has been setting the table admirably for a Cleveland club not getting as much as usual from third baseman José Ramírez (94 wRC+) and could help the Guardians secure not only the division title but a key first-round bye.
Jackson Merrill, Padres
Merrill took a step back in 2025 after finishing second to the Pirates’ Paul Skenes in 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award voting, and the Padres center fielder appeared headed for further regression based on early returns in 2026. Merrill’s OPS was below .600 in late May as San Diego scuffled offensively, and he took a .219/.278/.350 slash line into the break.
Since then, Merrill has been a major reason why the Padres have a 38-21 (.644) record in the second half, tied with the Brewers for the best in the NL. He’s hitting .312 with 16 home runs, 48 RBIs and a .944 OPS in 59 games in the second half while playing standout defense in center. Merrill’s ability to recapture his rookie form has given the Padres a fighting chance to host a Wild Card Series, and he’ll be a key middle-of-the-order bat for the club.
George Springer, Blue Jays
Springer improved his OPS by nearly 300 points from 2024 to 2025, slashing .309/.399/.560 and finishing seventh in AL MVP balloting as Toronto fell just short of a World Series title. But the veteran’s numbers fell off again early in 2026, especially after Springer returned from a stint on the injured list for a left big toe fracture. He hit just .218 with a .677 OPS before the All-Star break, a period of rest that seemed to help considerably.
Springer recorded multiple hits in five of his first nine second-half games, finishing July with an .878 OPS, before batting .321 with an .858 OPS in August. While he has slowed a bit in September, battling multiple injuries, he has clearly found his footing at the plate. It might not be enough to drag a Blue Jays team dealing with a host of pitching injuries and a down year from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. to the postseason, but Toronto -- three games out of an AL Wild Card spot -- still has a chance.
Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres
While Merrill’s turnaround has been integral to the Padres’ second-half surge, Tatis’ production out of the leadoff spot has perhaps been even more important. The three-time All-Star began the season by scorching the baseball into the ground, going 55 games before hitting his first home run of the year on May 30.
The second half brought on a true power surge for Tatis, who homered three times in his first four games after the All-Star break and is now up to 24 dingers on the season. Entering Saturday, his 167 wRC+ in the second half was second in MLB, behind only Bregman. Tatis has raised his season OPS to .819 and has given the Padres a dangerous option at leadoff down the stretch.
Pitchers
Brayan Bello, Red Sox
Bello has turned the page on a dismal start to the season. The right-hander, coming off a 3.35 ERA as a starter in 2025, had a 9.00 ERA in his first six starts of 2026 and was moved to a bulk-relief role. Still, Bello took a 6.06 ERA into the All-Star break as the Red Sox finally began to heat up, winning nine straight games to end the first half and extending the streak to a franchise record-tying 15.
Bello has continued to impress for Boston, earning the start on Saturday and baffling the Rays over eight innings of one-run ball with 11 strikeouts. In the midst of a statistically unprecedented season, he’s found something that works, which has been crucial for a Red Sox team that has surged into postseason position and appears headed for another clash with the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series.
Robert Gasser, Brewers
Tommy John surgery in June 2024 cut short Gasser’s promising rookie season, but he returned to make two solid starts at the tail end of 2025. The left-hander couldn’t sustain that success early in 2026, taking a 5.24 ERA into the All-Star break after being tagged for seven runs in three innings in his final first-half start.
Since then, Gasser has a 3.00 ERA in 57 innings of work after holding the Orioles scoreless over seven excellent innings on Saturday in Baltimore. In his first four September outings, including two against the Cubs, he has allowed just four earned runs across 21 innings pitched. With Brandon Woodruff’s 2026 return questionable and Kyle Harrison struggling mightily, Gasser’s improvement has made him an important arm for a Milwaukee team fighting to secure the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Tyler Mahle, Braves
Mahle owned a 5.13 ERA through his first 18 starts of 2026 for the Giants, but the Braves saw something in the veteran right-hander. Atlanta acquired Mahle ahead of the Trade Deadline for righty reliever Anthony Molina in a move that has paid considerable dividends for the Braves’ battered rotation.
Mahle has allowed only seven earned runs in eight starts for Atlanta, completing six or more innings in all but one of those outings. His 1.28 ERA in that span is the third best among all pitchers (min. 40 innings), and he’s been an excellent complement to ace lefty Chris Sale atop the Braves rotation. With Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo López and Hurston Waldrep all on the injured list, Mahle has not only covered important innings but has been remarkably effective.
Aaron Nola, Phillies
Nola had an ERA above 6 in an injury-marred 2025 season, and his 2026 looked to be more of the same. The usually dependable right-hander gave up 20 home runs in the first half alone, tied for the fifth most in MLB, and headed into the All-Star break with a 5.75 ERA.
Since then, Nola has returned to near-vintage form for the Phillies, who have also gotten strong second halves from lefty Jesús Luzardo (currently on the injured list with left shoulder inflammation) and rookie righty Andrew Painter. After Thursday’s excellent start against the Mets, Nola has a 2.78 ERA in the second half, striking out 67 in 71 1/3 innings despite giving up 14 more home runs in just 12 starts. If he can limit the long balls, he could be at least an adequate replacement for Luzardo if the southpaw cannot return for the start of the postseason.
Brandon Pfaadt, D-backs
Pfaadt hasn’t quite lived up to his billing as a former top prospect just yet, but he’s shown flashes, such as his success against the Dodgers and Phillies during the D-backs’ 2023 World Series run. The righty's recent results have been quite encouraging, too: Pfaadt has a 3.01 ERA in the second half, including a run of 27 2/3 scoreless innings across four starts from July 28-Aug. 14. 
Optioned to Triple-A Reno in June after a poor start to the year, Pfaadt now has the chance to help pitch the D-backs into the playoffs, which might be difficult in an NL Wild Card race featuring the Cubs, Phillies and Padres. Pfaadt is lined up to start during Arizona’s final series of the season, a pivotal three-game set in San Diego from Sept. 25-27, and his outing could determine the D-backs’ postseason fate.

Early season struggles are not necessarily new to Alex Bregman. Throughout his career, the season has generally played out in varying levels of fine in the early-going before the production catches fire in July & August. In his first season with the Chicago Cubs, though, things certainly reached a point where we were all left wondering if that typical summer ascent was actually going to manifest.
While Bregman's numbers were otherwise respectable throughout those first three months of the year, he also wasn't providing much in terms of impact. A .243/.343/.347 line kept him close to respectability (97 wRC+), but he also maintained an ISO of only .103 across more than 380 plate appearances. We heard plenty about adjustments being made, but the absence of notable contributions for a player consistently hitting in the two, three, or four holes in the lineup became a glaring shortcoming for the team.
That was particularly true after June. In that month, Bregman slashed just .200/.348/.300 with a 16.5 percent walk rate serving as effectively the one thing keeping him afloat production-wise. Batted ball luck didn't help either, with Bregman going for a BABIP of just .211.
Something happened when the calendar flipped over to July, though.
Bregman has caught fire in a way that very few players throughout the league could match. In roughly 300 plate appearances since July 1, he's at a .291/.368/.598 line with 19 homers, a gaudy .307 ISO, and a 163 wRC+. He's been one of the best hitters the sport has to offer over that stretch, to the point where the whole season numbers land him in fifth among National League position players in fWAR (5.2).
What's even wilder about the turnaround is that there haven't been a whole host of mechanical changes to indicate such a torrid pace since July, which one might typically expect when hearing a term like "adjustments."
Instead, the mechanics have remained steady. Bregman's bat speed and tilt are each identical between his plate appearances into the end of June and the ones that have come since the start of July. His attack angle and attack direction have each shifted by about two degrees, with the swing getting flatter (15 degrees through June 30 vs. 13 degrees since) and favoring a direction closer to center (six degrees through June 30th and four degrees since). It's not a tremendous difference, but one that speaks to his biggest shift (to which we'll get in a moment) on some level. Further, he's moved within the box but only slightly, with each of his depth and distance from the plate increasing by barely more than an inch.
None of these numbers are particularly notable in the grand scheme of things. Had the player been performing at a consistent level throughout the season, we may not have even noticed them at all. Instead, Bregman's shift since his inflection point at the June-July point in the calendar looks to be the result of timing more than anything else.
This is Bregman's swing timing against the three main pitch groups through June 30th:
Bregman was largely in the proper windows against fastballs, but struggles began to present themselves against the other two types. Notably, he was early on off-speed and breaking pitches while some of the contact against breaking pitches specifically spilled toward the end of the bat more frequently than one might like. Which is why it's no surprise that his ability to make quality contact was stifled quite a bit; in April & June, his hard-hit rate against breaking pitches checked in at only 25.9 percent. You're not going to find any level of batted ball luck that way.
Here, however, is Bregman since July 1:
The vertical component of his timing was never really in question against any pitch group. What Bregman has managed to do, though, is rein in the horizontal point of contact and generate swings that are more on time in terms of his bat's placement within the zone upon contact. The two subsequent months saw him increase his rate of hard contact against breaking pitches.
In general, though, this is just a professional hitter doing professional hitter things. At no point this year has Bregman gotten out of his approach or overhauled his mechanics to look for a solution that didn't necessarily need to be found. The approach remained intact and continues to get even better, considering he's walking nearly twice as often this month (11.5 percent) as he's striking out (6.6 percent). This was almost all a matter of timing. It's not purely that—consider the slight change in his bat path—but it's allowed those changes that would otherwise be marginal or entirely unnoticed to actually have some level of impact.
The reality is that we were always going to see this form from Alex Bregman eventually. Maybe not to this extent on the power side of things, but while we may have this perception of two different version of Bregman in 2026, he remains very much the same player he's always been.
